## ⚠️⚠️⚠️ TIER 0-A — PUBLISH THE PODCAST AUDIO. THE OWNER'S HIGHEST PRIORITY, SET 8 SEPTEMBER 2026.

**Owner's ask:** make the audio downloadable from the site; publish to Spotify with a link back to the
site; support players like BookPlayer; put a clear link to the audio version at the top of each page
(or a Spotify player — whichever is easiest for users and looks good); add a dedicated section to the
downloads page; decide whether MP3 is needed for Spotify or better in general; and enrich the file
metadata so the files behave well in Apple Music and similar.

### What is on disk — MEASURED 8 September 2026, not carried. Re-measure before acting.

| | |
|---|---|
| files | **37 `.m4a`**, in 8 directories matching the corpus's sections |
| total | **37.2 hours · 4.31 GB** |
| codec | **AAC, 44.1 kHz, STEREO, ~257 kbps** |
| longest | 72.1 min (`Hockey IQ/Risk Management and Decision-Making.m4a`, 139 MB) |
| metadata | ⚠️ **NONE.** Every file carries only `major_brand`, `minor_version`, `compatible_brands`, `creation_time`, `encoder`. **No title, artist, album, track, date, genre, artwork or chapters.** |
| in git? | **No** — `.gitignore:46-47` cover `*.m4a` and `*.mp3`. ⚠️ **The `podcasts/` DIRECTORY is not ignored, only the extensions. A `.wav`, `.opus` or artwork file dropped in there WOULD be committable.** |
| tooling | `ffmpeg` and `ffprobe` present at `/opt/homebrew/bin/` |

### ⚠️ The decisions to make, and the facts that bear on them

**1. Bitrate. 257 kbps stereo is 4-8× what spoken word needs.** Mono AAC at 64 kbps is a normal
speech setting and would take the library from ~4.31 GB to roughly 1 GB. **This is the single biggest
lever on hosting cost, CDN egress and how long a phone takes to download an episode**, and it is worth
deciding before anything else is built. Verify by ear on one file before committing to it.

**2. ⚠️ MP3 vs M4A is a GENERATION-LOSS question, not just a compatibility one.** These files are
already lossy AAC. **Transcoding AAC → MP3 decodes and re-encodes, and the artefacts compound.** If a
higher-quality master exists (from whatever produced them — see `.claude/skills/notebooklm-episode`),
re-encode from THAT, not from these. If these are the masters, prefer keeping AAC and emitting MP3 only
where a platform genuinely requires it. **Do not transcode the whole library to MP3 as a default.**

**3. ⚠️ M4B and chapters are the real prize for BookPlayer and Apple Books.** M4B is the audiobook
container — same AAC audio, different extension — and it carries **chapter marks and resume position**.
A 72-minute episode with no chapters is much worse to use than the same episode with them.

⚠️⚠️ **BUT THE ROUTE THIS ROW ORIGINALLY GAVE FOR GETTING THEM IS FALSE, AND IT WAS NEVER TESTED
BEFORE IT WAS WRITTEN DOWN.** It read: *"the corpus already has section headings, and
`scripts/md_to_speech.py` already knows where they fall, so chapter marks are derivable from work
already done."* **Measured 9 September 2026 against `podcasts_web/manifest.json` and the corpus:**

| document | episode | words | apparent wpm |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reading Ice Hockey Diagrams | 53.4 min | 4,198 | **79** |
| Rules Primer | 67.9 min | 93,153 | **1,371** |
| whole library | 37.2 h | 1,164,940 | 522 |

Speech runs ~150 wpm. ⚠️ **Every one of the 37 episodes lands in a 48-72 minute band REGARDLESS of
whether its document is 4,198 words or 93,153** — a 17x spread in apparent rate. **The duration is a
property of the production, not of the text. No episode is a complete reading of its document, and
there is no mapping from a heading to a timestamp.** `md_to_speech.py`'s section boundaries are
positions in TEXT; chapters need positions in AUDIO, and nothing on disk relates the two.

**Owner's decision, 9 September 2026: derive chapters FROM THE AUDIO** — transcribe each episode,
place marks at real topic boundaries. ⚠️ **That is a new pipeline, not a reuse of existing work: no
transcription tooling is installed** (no `whisper`, `whisper-cpp`, `faster_whisper`, `mlx_whisper` or
`torch` — checked), and 37.2 hours must be transcribed and **every boundary reviewed before it ships**.

**4. The site already has the patterns to reuse.** `site/src/pages/downloads.astro` has EPUB, PDF and
Markdown sections with a `download-list` class and per-file notes; `scripts/build-downloads.mjs` writes
`dist/downloads/manifest.json` **carrying byte sizes**, which an audio section should use so a reader
sees "88 MB" before tapping on mobile data.

**5. ⚠️ A PODCAST FEED CANNOT BE THE EXISTING FEED, AND THE REASON IS RECORDED IN THE EXISTING ONE.**
`site/src/pages/rss.xml.ts` is hand-rolled RSS 2.0 with **zero** iTunes-namespace elements and **zero**
enclosures, and it **deliberately emits no `pubDate`** — its own comment says the corpus *"is a book, not
a blog"*, that a build-time date *"is a claim the build cannot support"*, and that dating it would
*"republish all 37 to every subscriber"* on every rebuild. ⚠️ **Podcast clients sort by date and
generally require an enclosure per item.** So this needs a **separate** feed, and the date problem has to
be solved deliberately — stable synthetic dates that never change on rebuild, or `itunes:season` /
`itunes:episode` ordering. **Do not "fix" the existing feed by adding dates to it; that decision is
already made and reasoned.** Note also the site's stated policy of **exactly one production dependency** —
a hand-rolled podcast feed matches the house pattern.

**6. Hosting.** Deployment is S3 + CloudFront (`infra/`). 4.31 GB of audio, or ~1 GB re-encoded, changes
the egress profile materially. ⚠️ **`infra/` is do-not-run and owner-approval territory.**

### ⚠️ MEASURED: THE STEREO IS FAKE. Mono costs nothing.

Phase-inverted sum of the two channels over a 60-second excerpt of
`Off the Ice/Equipment.m4a`:

| | |
|---|---|
| L − R difference signal | **−91.0 dB** — the noise floor |
| the content itself | **−26.8 dB** |

**A 64 dB gap. The channels are identical: these are dual-mono files carried in a stereo container.**
⚠️ **So roughly half of the 257 kbps is spent encoding a duplicate of the other channel, and converting
to mono discards NOTHING — it is not a quality trade at all.** That is why mono is the first cut to
take and why it does not touch the owner's "must still sound great" condition.

**Measured library projections, from 90-second excerpts encoded at each setting**
(samples in `podcasts/_bitrate_samples/`, gitignored by extension — **listen before choosing**):

| setting | of original | library | a 70-min episode |
|---|---|---|---|
| original 257k stereo | 100% | 4.31 GB | ~142 MB |
| 128k stereo | 50% | 2.16 GB | ~71 MB |
| **96k mono** | **39%** | **1.68 GB** | **~56 MB** |
| 80k mono | 33% | 1.40 GB | ~46 MB |
| 64k mono | 26% | 1.12 GB | ~37 MB |

⚠️ **Because the source is dual mono, "96k mono" is not a downgrade from "128k stereo" — it is MORE bits
per actual channel of audio.** A conservative choice that clearly satisfies "still sounds great" is
**96k or 128k mono**; 64k mono is where speech artefacts usually start to become audible on good
headphones. **Decide by listening to the samples, not from this table.**

### Multi-client access — the shapes to build, mirroring a pattern the site already has

⚠️ **`downloads.astro` already offers EPUB and PDF as "The complete corpus" PLUS one per section. The
audio should mirror that exactly**, because it is the house pattern and it answers "different users with
different clients" directly:

| client / user | what they need |
|---|---|
| **Podcast apps** (Apple Podcasts, Overcast, Pocket Casts) | an **RSS feed with `<enclosure>`s** and the `itunes:` namespace |
| **Spotify** | the show, submitted from that feed, plus a link back to the site |
| **BookPlayer / Apple Books** | **M4B with chapters** — per section, and one for the whole corpus |
| **VLC, Apple Music, car stereos, generic players** | an **`.m3u` / `.m3u8` playlist** referencing the episode URLs — universal, trivial to generate, and the single cheapest win on this list |
| **"just give me everything"** | a **ZIP of all 37**, with the size stated before the click |
| **on the page, one episode** | a self-hosted `<audio>` element or a download link |

⚠️ **An `.m3u` playlist is one text file and covers most desktop clients. Do it early; it is the highest
ratio of user benefit to work on this whole row.**

⚠️ **A whole-corpus M4B with chapters is the BookPlayer/Apple Books answer AND the "list of episodes"
answer at once** — 37 chapters in one file, resumable. ⚠️ **Those 37 chapter marks ARE derivable
without a transcript, because they are FILE boundaries and the manifest already carries every
duration.** ⚠️ **Do not confuse them with WITHIN-episode chapters, which are not derivable at all —
see the refutation above.** This row previously asserted the latter.

### ⚠️⚠️⚠️ OPEN — A MANUAL BUILT ON A SUPERSEDED RULEBOOK IS AN AUTHORITY IN THREE PLACES, AND ITS DATE IS RECORDED IN NONE

USA Hockey's *Introduction To Body Contact* (`sources/ibc.txt`) attributes its body-check definition to the
**"USA Hockey 2007-09 Official Rules of Ice Hockey"** at `ibc.txt:152`. `sources/README.md:41` records it as
the authority behind two claims and **does not record that**.

⚠️ **THE COORDINATOR CALLED IT "FIFTEEN YEARS OLD" IN THE REPAIR BRIEF AND THAT FIGURE CAME FROM NOWHERE.**
The repairing agent refused to write it, reporting that the manual carries **no publication year anywhere in
the extracted text** — its only edition marker is the rulebook it quotes. It dated the manual by that
rulebook instead, which is on disk and checkable. **A year count invented by a dispatcher is a fabricated
figure however small the error**, and this is the second brief defect recorded in this round.

**The two datable facts, both verified 10 September 2026, neither of them a stated publication date:**
`grep -oE '\b(19|20)[0-9]{2}\b' sources/ibc.txt | sort -u` returns **`2007` and nothing else**, and
`pdfinfo sources/ibc.pdf` gives **CreationDate Thu Jul 22 2010**. ⚠️ **PDF creation metadata is when a file
was written, not when a document was published, and it is trivially wrong on re-exported PDFs** — so it
corroborates the 2007-09 attribution rather than replacing it. **Cite the rulebook the manual quotes. That
is the fact that bears on whether its content is current, which is the only thing anyone needs from it.**

**Found because one of its claims had gone stale in exactly the way a dated manual does.** `mental_game.md`
relayed its age-group progression as *"only introduces body checking at 12-and-Under"* — while the current
`usah.txt:3555` Rule 604(a) **prohibits** body checking at 12 & under. That site is being repaired.

⚠️ **THE OTHER TWO WERE NOT CHECKED AND ARE NOT KNOWN TO BE WRONG.** `sources/README.md:41` names the same
manual as the authority behind **the open-ice check one-stride condition** and **the §6 boards three-case
rule**, both in `body_contact_and_battles.md`. Nobody has asked whether either moved between the 2007-09
book and the current one. **A safety reviewer explicitly handed this over rather than filing it**, which is
the correct call and also means it is now nobody's unless it is written down.

**The class, which is the point:** a source can be accurately quoted, correctly cited, and still wrong,
because the BOOK IT DESCRIBES has moved. No checker in this repository can see that — `check_links`,
`check_facts` and `check_disclosures` all passed this document, and the quotation was faithful. **The tell
is the source's DATE, and `sources/README.md` does not carry dates for every entry.**

**Next:** date every `sources/` entry that describes another document's rules, then re-test the two
`body_contact_and_battles.md` claims against the current USA Hockey book.

### ⚠️ OPEN — the IIHF penalty shot is WIDER than the NHL's, and the divergence is written down nowhere

`rules-verifier` confirmed every citation in `risk_management.md`'s new breakaway `Rule:` line and rated it
**confirmed-but-incomplete** on one point. IIHF 24.8 criterion (II), at `iihf_rules_v1.1.txt:2461-2462`:

> *"(II) The infraction must have been committed from behind **(except a foul committed from the front by
> the goalkeeper on a "breakaway" situation)**;"*

The NHL's matching criterion (`nhl_rules.txt:6443`) is bare. **So the IIHF awards a penalty shot in a case
the NHL does not**, and the corpus's *"the IIHF writes it at 24.8"* reads as *identical*. Present in the
2026/27 book too.

⚠️ **Direction of harm is UNDERSTATEMENT, not danger** — a reader misses an entitlement rather than earning
a penalty — which is why no reviewer stopped on it. The document already carries the equivalent divergence
for USA Hockey (*"diagonally from behind"*) and Hockey Canada (*"or fouled by the goaltender"*) at `:463`
and `:851`. **The IIHF's is the one not written down**, and the IIHF is the book a British reader is under.

**Also recorded from the same report, neither adjudicated:** the document's *"you"* is the FOULER in the new
facts line and the FOULED player at `:479` and `:486` — both correct, not the same person, and only the
surrounding section disambiguates, which a listener does not get. And *"a 21% minor"* uses a rate whose
denominator is **power-play opportunities, which include double minors and majors**, as the price of a
minor — a proxy the document does not label as one. The style guide records 21.1% as having **no owner**.

### ⚠️⚠️ A REVIEWER'S REPORT IS A BRIEF TOO — the coordinator relayed a reviewer's error and it survived into a second brief

**10 September 2026.** A `site-reviewer` reported a build/index divergence in `mental_game.md` as:

> dist carries *"neither the IIHF book nor the In-House Rules states an age"*; the index carries *"no British
> source publishes an age at all"*.

**The two are the wrong way round.** `git log -S` puts *"no British source publishes an age at all"* in
**cfedea3 (31 August)** — it is the **retired** wording. The **staged** text is *"neither the IIHF book nor
the In-House Rules states an age"*, and the retired phrasing was a negative-existence claim **the same
sentence contradicts**, because it goes on to quote IHUK's Rules of Competition putting the junior line
between U12 and U14.

⚠️ **The coordinator carried it into the NEXT brief verbatim, as the string to adjudicate.** The second
`site-reviewer` refuted it against the repository and said so plainly: *"the brief has the two strings
backwards… the expectation in the brief would have failed the page for rendering the correct text."*

**The lesson is not "check reviewer reports."** It is that ⚠️ **"refute the brief" has been read as aimed at
PLAN ROWS, and a REVIEWER'S REPORT is the one input that arrives already looking like verified evidence** —
it names files, quotes strings, cites line numbers. **That is exactly what makes relaying it unexamined
dangerous.** The corpus was never wrong here; both briefs were. **A finding is a claim until the next agent
re-derives it, and the coordinator is the one who turns a claim into an instruction.**

**Cost this time: nothing, because the receiving agent re-derived.** That is the second time in two rounds
the method has been saved by the agent rather than by the dispatcher.

### ⚠️ OPEN — five carried findings from the `mental_game.md` 12U repair, none of them the repair's own defect

The repair was upheld on every tested point. These are what the reviewer found around it.

⚠️ **M3 IS THE ONE THAT WILL BITE SOMEBODY. THE REPAIR'S STATED SAFETY MECHANISM IS NOT THE ONE THAT WORKS.**
The repairing agent reported the ⚠️ marker *"hoists to 'Important.' at the paragraph head BEFORE the age is
spoken"*. It does — **but ~1,200 characters earlier, at the head of a 2,229-character paragraph**, where a
listener attaches it to graded exposure in general. **What actually protects the listener is that the 12U
claim and its 604(a) correction are ONE SENTENCE**, so no sentence-boundary split the chunker can make can
separate them. That is stronger than "one chunk" — and it means a future editor may move or reword the
hoisted marker freely, but **may NOT separate *"do not take the ages from it"* from the age sentence, and
may NOT split the 12U claim from the 604(a) clause.** Recorded because the next editor would otherwise be
told the wrong thing is load-bearing.

**M1 — the edition note understates the evidence it has.** `mental_game.md:718` says *"No publication date
appears in the extracted text"*, which is TRUE — `sources/ibc.txt` holds exactly one four-digit year, `2007`,
and greps for `copyright|©|published|printed|edition|revised` return nothing, against a healthy 3.2%
text-to-PDF ratio. But `pdfinfo sources/ibc.pdf` gives `CreationDate Thu Jul 22 2010`, `Producer
QuarkXPress 8.1`. ⚠️ **This is the *"makes the corpus look LESS supported than it is"* direction.** If the
metadata date is added it must be labelled **file metadata, not a publication date**, and the conclusion must
not move: the 2007-09 quotation stays the load-bearing evidence, because a QuarkXPress timestamp does not
establish an edition. **And `check_disclosures.py` does NOT flag line 718** — a textbook absence-of-evidence
claim, in an unvoiced layer, invisible to the tool built to find exactly those.

⚠️ **AND THE GREP MAY BE THE WRONG INSTRUMENT.** The reviewer did **not** render `ibc.pdf`'s 60 pages with
`pdftoppm`. **A publication date printed on a cover or colophon lives only in the page images**, and a text
grep is structurally incapable of seeing it — the exact failure `sources/README.md` documents for `crt6`.
Render it before anyone calls this manual undated again.

**M2 — the new British sentence reduces Britain to an age-group lookup.** `mental_game.md:377` sends a reader
to *"which format your competition's Rules of Competition set for your age group"*. But
`body_contact_and_battles.md` §1 states *"In the senior game the league decides it, not your age"*, and NIHL
D1/D2 status sits in a divisional ROC **with no age column**. An adult British reader looks for an age group
and finds none — and the framing sits at odds with the repair's own core clause, which exists to say age is
only half of it. Mitigated by the §1 link; failure direction is over-caution.

**M4 — chunk 026 is at ~2,677 billed characters against `MAX_BILLED_CHARS = 2800`. About 123 characters of
headroom**, so the next edit to that section forces a re-chunk. Safe, because of the atomic-sentence property
in M3 — but this chunk is in `--near` territory and nobody was tracking it.

**M5 — Common Mistakes carries no checking caveat, and that is CORRECT.** Recorded as a decision rather than
an oversight: Common Mistakes never raises checking at all, so there is no naked instruction there to
counterweight. Both places the hazard IS raised carry the byte-identical caveat.

### ⚠️ OPEN — *"Angling, by contrast, is legal in every league"* is an unscoped absolute, and CARHA may be the exception

`mental_game.md:121`, pre-existing and untouched by the 12U repair. USA Hockey 604's Note blesses angling
explicitly (`usah.txt:3577-3581`). **CARHA has no such carve-out:** Rule 49(a) penalises a player who *"does
not avert body contact with an opponent"* and 49(c) excuses only *"accidental contact"*, so angling that
closes to deliberate contact is penalisable under CARHA as written.

Angling as pure steering without contact is legal everywhere, which is probably what the sentence means —
**but "in every league" is an unscoped absolute in a corpus that scopes them everywhere else, and
`check_absolutes.py` passes it.** Decide whether the tool should see this shape, or whether the sentence
should say what it means.

### ⚠️⚠️⚠️ STANDING — "REFUTE THE BRIEF" IS AIMED AT AGENTS, AND THE DISPATCHER IS EXEMPT FROM NOTHING

⚠️ **A citation copied out of an AGENT'S REPORT is exactly as unverified as a figure copied out of a
plan row, and the loop has never said so.**

**Measured, round 70.** A `rules-verifier` reported a passage as *"USA Hockey Rule 403 'GAME
MISCONDUCT'"*. The coordinator relayed that into a repair agent's brief **verbatim, without opening the
book**. The agent followed a brief that named a rule and quoted its text — correctly, by its own
lights — and propagated it to **five sites in one file and three in another**. It then **reached a
commit**, because a concurrent session committed the partial work. `commit-gate` caught it.

**The quoted text is Rule 404(b)** (`usah.txt:2528-2540`), the ordinary next-game suspension.
**403(b)** (`usah.txt:2440-2449`) is the **second major in the same game**, worth **two** games. ⚠️ **The
book distinguishes them explicitly** — 404(b) names 403(b) as its own exception — so it cites the
two-game case for a one-game consequence. ⚠️ **And five other documents already had it right**, so the
diff shipped a self-contradiction.

**THE RULE THAT COMES OUT OF IT, and it is the counterpart to the instruction that already does the most
work here:**

> ⚠️ **Every rule number, quotation and figure the coordinator puts INTO a brief must be re-derived from
> primary text by the coordinator, or explicitly flagged in the brief as unverified relay.**
> "Refute the brief" cannot save an agent from a citation that is wrong in a way only the book reveals,
> because the agent's own verification will confirm the QUOTE — the quote is real — while the NUMBER
> attached to it is not. **A correct quotation under a wrong citation passes every check an agent runs.**

⚠️ **This is the fourth recorded instance of a wrong premise entering through a brief, and the first
where the premise came from another agent's report rather than from the plan.** The plan already
warns that relayed site lists measured 33-75% short and that one brief carried four distinct errors.
**Add this shape to that list: a relayed CITATION, correct in its text and wrong in its number.**

`site/src/diagrams/*.mjs`. Captions are SPOKEN.** `playing_without_the_puck.mjs` still carried
*"Never meet a goal post head first, and never duck — head up, chin off your chest."* while all three
`content/` copies were already in the repaired form. **Same sentence, repaired in the layer people read,
left standing in the layer people hear** — and the module's comment quoted the *pre-repair* wording as
its source, so it would have survived the next review too, with a citation.

⚠️ **Assume every past corpus-wide sweep has this hole.** Ask what the sweep's grep could not see:
`site/src/diagrams/*.mjs`, `site/src/data/diagrams.json`, the `describe` fields, and `project/`.

   InDesign slug, `:3568` the running head, `:3569-3570` two blanks. **Quoting text out of a `sed` window
   verifies the TEXT, not the ADDRESS.**
2. **Carrying a line number in from a brief** instead of re-deriving it.
3. ⚠️ **NEW — a `grep -n` on a clause-opening string is NOT automatically an address.** USA Hockey **reuses

   opener 14**. ⚠️ **It must return ONE hit, or be pinned by a second anchor.** **The verifier committed
   mechanism 1 itself (`:2934` for `:2936`) while writing up mechanism 1 — the instruction is load-bearing on
   the verifier, not only on the dispatcher.**

**SETTLED, each by a single-hit `grep -n`:** 604 Note 1 `:3543-3545` · 604(a) list `:3555-3558` · furniture
`:3563`, `:3567`, `:3568` · **local-governing-body limb `:3571-3573`** · Note `:3574-3576` · 604(b) `:3577-3579`
· 604(c) `:3580-3581` · 604(d) `:3594-3596` · 604(e) `:3597-3599` · 411(a) `:2913-2915` · **604 on the

components — skates parallel · forearm and hip · head up · chin off your chest — must survive any repair.**
**Dispatched to `safety-reviewer` 10 September 2026** with four routes: shorten the **reason** clause not the
instruction; give the fragment its own verb; split the section; or re-cut an existing value.

### ✅ RESOLVED 10 September 2026 — NHL 81.1 vs 81.6 is **NOT** a citation divergence. Both are right.

A reviewer found the shorthanded-icing exemption cited to **81.1** at `breakouts.md:87`/`:99` and to **81.6**
at `:433`/`:447` and in ten sites across four other documents, and **correctly refused to adjudicate it from
the corpus** — *"verifying it by reading another corpus document is exactly the mechanism this defect class
propagates through."* **Settled by the coordinator against `sources/nhl_rules.txt`:**

- **81.1 Icing** — *"Should any player of a team, **equal or superior in numerical strength (power-play)** to
  the opposing team, shoot, bat or deflect the puck from his own half of the ice beyond the goal line…"*
  **The exemption is IMPLICIT in 81.1's scope**, and `:87` quotes that phrase, so citing 81.1 is right.
- **81.6 Numerical Strength** — *"If the puck was so shot by a player of a side **below the numerical
  strength** of the opposing team, play shall continue and the icing violation shall not be called."*
  **The exemption stated EXPLICITLY**, so citing 81.6 is right too.

⚠️ **Two correct citations for two different things. Nothing to fix, and a sweep would have destroyed a
correct distinction.**

⚠️ **BUT 81.6 CARRIES TWO FURTHER LIMBS, AND THEY ARE THE PART THAT CATCHES A PLAYER OUT:**
> *"When a team is 'short-handed' as the result of a penalty and the penalty is about to expire, the decision
> as to whether there has been an 'icing' shall be determined **at the instant the penalty expires**. Should
> the puck be released from the stick of the player shooting the puck down the ice **prior to the penalty
> expiring, the icing infraction shall not apply**. The action of the penalized player remaining in the
> penalty box will not alter the ruling. When a team is 'short-handed' by reason of a **major** penalty, and
> they have neglected to ensure there is a player on the penalty bench to exit upon the expiry of the
> penalty, they will continue to play shorthanded **but are not permitted to ice the puck**."*

**Coordinator census: the expiry limb is carried in `rules_primer.md` and `special_teams.md` — the two right
owners.** ⚠️ **NOT a gap. Recorded so nobody re-opens it.**

| **A LADDER** (two or more rungs in one value) | ⚠️ ***"is"*** | *"clause a **is** a minor, … clause b **is** a major"* — **the verb marks where the citation ends and the tier begins** |
| **A PREPOSITIONAL PHRASE** (*"under Hockey Canada 6.2(c)…"*) | ⚠️ **comma — *"is"* is IMPOSSIBLE** | *"clause c **is** the minor is mandatory"* — **ungrammatical. Only the comma works.** |
| **A SINGLE citation plus tier** | **comma** | *"clause a, a minor"* — clean appositive, ⚠️ **and eleven values already used it. DO NOT SWEEP THOSE.** |

**The comma agent's case:** the renderer already emits a comma **before** *"clause"*, so a following comma
gives a clean appositive; *"is "* costs 3 characters; and ⚠️ **it cannot be used at all in the prepositional
cases.** **Settled for it by finding `breakouts.md:257` already using the comma.**
**The *"is"* agent's case:** ⚠️ **it is the BODY's own form** (`body_contact_and_battles.md:520-529` already
writes *"7.4(a) is a mandatory bare minor"*), ⚠️ **it was already HALF-APPLIED inside the very lines it was
sent to fix** (*"608(b) **is** a mandatory major…, 7.5(c) a match penalty"* — one rung with the verb, the next
without), and **in a ladder the comma form gives seven commas in a row with nothing separating citation from
tier.**
⚠️ **AND WHERE THE FRAME WOULD NOT TAKE A VERB IT CHANGED THE FRAME RATHER THAN THE FORM** — *"prices
charging at 7.4(a) a minor"* → *"prices charging this way — 7.4(a) is a minor"*. ⚠️ **It also refused to write
*"three tiers"*, because `hc_layout.txt:4773-4791` shows 7.4 runs (a) to (e) and a rung count would have been
an authored claim.**

**Coordinator audit of the result: 25 values now use *"is"*, and exactly ONE comma-in-a-ladder remains**
(`forechecking_systems.md:553`). ⚠️ **READ AND ACCEPTED, NOT SWEPT: it separates its books with SEMICOLONS,
which do the boundary work the verb would otherwise do.**

⚠️ **THE DISPATCHER'S CENSUS WAS BADLY SHORT AND BOTH AGENTS SAID SO.** The brief said **30 corpus-wide,
seven** in one agent's files. Measured by rendering: **25 bare instances across 17 lines in those five files
alone**, and ⚠️ **40 stutters rendered in `body_contact_and_battles.md` ALONE, against nine allotted.** The
other agent found **four** where the brief said two, **plus seven more by sweeping its own six.**
**Facts layer: 25 → 0. Body and summary prose: ~53 remain, deliberately untouched — those sit inside long
sentences where surrounding words carry the parse, and a corpus-wide decision there is the coordinator's.**

`goaltender.md:856`/`:867` said ***"🇬🇧 The IIHF adds a provision the NHL does not."*** ⚠️ **NHL Rule 24.2
CONTAINS IT WORD FOR WORD:**

> *"The team against whom the penalty shot has been assessed may replace their goalkeeper to defend against
> the shot, however, the substitute goalkeeper is required to remain in the game until the next stoppage of
> play."*

IIHF text is identical apart from quotation marks round *"Penalty Shot"*.

THE FIRST TIME: THE SENTENCE STRADDLES A PAGE BREAK, SPLICED WITH A RUNNING HEADER AND A PAGE NUMBER, SO A
GREP FOR THE WHOLE SENTENCE RETURNS ZERO.** ⚠️ **A grep for the FRAGMENT `substitute goalkeeper is required`
finds it in every extraction.** **Repaired under NN3 — a primary source contradicts the claim — and the 🇬🇧
flag was dropped, because the flag marks a British divergence and there is none.**

⚠️ **`rules-verifier` SHOULD SWEEP FOR OTHER *"X adds a provision Y does not"* CLAIMS, and for any rule whose
text crosses a page break in the NHL extraction. ONE was checked.**

on its own initiative and stumbled on this one while verifying something else. ONE OF TWO TESTED CAME BACK
FALSE. *"That is not a base rate — I picked one because it was safety-bearing and stumbled on the other — but
it is a reason to think the remaining negatives in these files are under-attacked, and the one I found was
protected by the same page-break extraction trap that will protect others."***

### ⚠️⚠️⚠️ CLASS FINDING — **THE COORDINATOR'S PROPOSED WORDING WOULD HAVE INTRODUCED A CONTRADICTION, AND ONLY THE AGENT CAUGHT IT**

**The standing instruction is *"refute the brief before acting on it"*, and it has always been aimed at the
brief's PREMISES. This is the first recorded case of the brief's PROPOSED TEXT being the defect.**

The coordinator specified, for the CRT6 repair: *"do not go back on the ice — **or onto a bike, a board**, or
any other activity that could put your head into something — until a medical professional says you can."*

⚠️⚠️ **TWO PARAGRAPHS ABOVE, `:269` SETS OUT THE CONSENSUS GRADED RETURN-TO-SPORT PROGRESSION, WHOSE SECOND
STAGE IS LIGHT AEROBIC EXERCISE *BEFORE* MEDICAL CLEARANCE.** **Read aloud, the specified wording BANS A
STATIONARY BIKE and flatly contradicts the document's own protocol.**

**The agent rewrote it CRITERION-FIRST** — CRT6's *"risk of head contact, a fall or a collision"* stated
**before any example**, with examples chosen to be unambiguously risky (**mountain** bike, skateboard).
⚠️ **In its own words: *"This is the kind of contradiction only a whole-file diff catches, and it was
mine."*** — it was not; **it was the dispatcher's.**

⚠️ **THE LESSON, AND IT CHANGES HOW BRIEFS SHOULD BE WRITTEN: a coordinator specifying replacement TEXT is
writing content without having read the document. Specify the DEFECT and the CONSTRAINT; let the agent that
has read the file write the sentence — and when proposed wording IS supplied, say explicitly that it is a
sketch to be checked against the surrounding prose, not a string to paste.**

338, median 159, only 579 above 2,000. This is top ~1%, and the fifteen longest paragraphs in the corpus all
sit at 2,793-2,799 — the top of the distribution IS the chunk cap.**

**first after "Important."**, the floor caveat second. **A listener who disengages at thirty seconds has
both.**

⚠️ **WHAT DOES NOT SURVIVE IS THE ROUTING.** The 🇬🇧 flag starts around the **100-second mark of a
150-second utterance**, behind two North American rulebooks' worth of clause numbers. ⚠️ **And the split is
a CHARACTER CAP, not a meaning boundary: `015` ends on *"Women's hockey divides by book, and two of the four
make it blanket."* — a dangling promise whose answer is IN A DIFFERENT FILE.**
⚠️ **`check_chunk_tails` scans facts values and body prose but NOT BLOCKQUOTE INTERIORS. Nothing flagged
it.** **That is a tool gap, and it is open.**

**Fix dispatched: three consecutive blockquotes at seams the text already marks.** ⚠️ **Probed through the
real renderer rather than asserted — three consecutive blockquotes emit three separate `<p>` elements with a
500 ms break between each, and 🇬🇧 renders as *"For British readers."*, so each flag becomes its own
addressable utterance and the chunker gets three legal break points where it has none.**

will grow by the caption delta"*.**

### ⚠️⚠️⚠️ CLASS FINDING, 10 September 2026 — **THE WORKLIST WAS 87.6% OF THE LAYER, AND THE TOOL WAS MINE**

⚠️ **`check_caption_negations.py` HAD NEVER SCANNED 12.4% OF THE CAPTION LAYER.** `CAPTION` requires an
**uninterrupted run of quoted strings**, so a whole-line `//` comment inside a `'a' + 'b'` concatenation
**ended the run** and the tool scanned only the **prefix** of that caption.

**Measured, not asserted:** 55 caption/`describe` blocks in 27 modules carry inline `//` lines. The tool saw
**358,089 chars in 391 blocks**; comment-stripped assembly is **408,890 in 395**. **50,801 characters never
scanned**, hiding **156 hit occurrences — 4 at score 3 and 14 at score 2.**

⚠️ **AND IT WAS WORST EXACTLY WHERE IT MATTERS MOST — the safety-counterweight captions.**
`defending_the_rush.mjs` (44 comment lines) · `zone_entries.mjs` (39) · `forechecking_systems.mjs` (31, 30)
· `playing_without_the_puck.mjs` (30) · `body_contact_and_battles.mjs` (20) — and the crease caption in
`offensive_zone_play.mjs`, **three of whose inline comments are themselves records of previously-repaired
inversions.** ⚠️ **A round that "finished" this worklist would have finished the PREFIX.**

**FIXED 10 September 2026, three changes, all in the tool:**
1. `strip_line_comments()` — drops **whole-line** `//` only. ⚠️ **Whole-line only: a caption carrying
   `https://` loses half its text to a naive strip, and this corpus's captions do carry URLs.**
2. `IDENT` lookback **1500 → 4000**. At 1500, **13 of 68 hits reported as `[?]`** — unactionable on a
   worklist.
3. **The largest false-positive family, 16 of 68 (~24%): a MATCHED parenthetical scored as unmatched**,
   because `SHAPE` caps `mid` at 70 chars and `mid.count("—")` looked only inside that window. Now counts
   from the start of the **sentence**. ⚠️ **This SUPPRESSES hits, which is the dangerous direction — it is
   justified only because a matched pair genuinely defuses the carry, and it is recorded here so the
   suppression is on the record rather than in the diff.**

**Counts after the fix: 395 blocks in 31 modules · 582 occurrences · 7 suspicious · 65 worth a look.**
⚠️ **The pre-fix figures (391 · 496 · 6 · 68) are superseded. Do not quote them.**

⚠️ **THE HOUSE STYLE IS AT WAR WITH THE TOOL AND NEEDS AN OWNER'S RULING.** The corpus's own convention is
inline `// ⚠️ FULL STOP, NOT A COLON` notes **inside** caption concatenations — which is what blinded the
tool. The reviewer created two more instances while repairing findings and **reverted them**, moving its
rationale comments **above** `caption:`. **Fix 1 removes the conflict mechanically, but the convention
should still say where such a comment goes.**

on, skate behind the net"*, *"because the extra man is a body in front and not a sixth passer"*, *"in every
league, checking or not"*. ⚠️ **A subordinate negation does not carry, and a sweep would have "fixed" all
four.**

`@supports` scoping** — and the comment above asserts they cover different browsers: *"`scrollbar-color`
covers Firefox, the `::-webkit-scrollbar` block covers Chrome and Safari."* ⚠️ **Chrome honours the standard
property once it supports it and ignores the `::-webkit-scrollbar` block, so the comment is wrong about the
mechanism.**

⚠️ **BUT MEASURED BEFORE FILING, AND IT DOWNGRADES THIS: both paths set the SAME colours** (`--text-faint`
thumb, `--bg-raised` track). **So nothing is mis-coloured and nothing is invisible.** The only casualty is
the explicit `height: 10px`, which `scrollbar-width: thin` replaces. **Cosmetic — a dead block and a false
comment, not a broken scrollbar.**

**Fix:** correct the comment, and either scope the webkit block with `@supports not (scrollbar-color: auto)`
or delete it. ⚠️ **Needs a browser at 375px to confirm the thin bar is still usable on a phone — this is
the horizontal scroller on full-bleed diagrams, so it is the reader's only cue that the picture continues
off-screen.** Do not "fix" it by removing `scrollbar-color`: the comment records that the default overlay
bar fades out when idle, *"which is exactly when the reader needs to be told"*.

### ⚠️⚠️ THREE SITE MAJORS FOUND IN A BROWSER, ALL THREE INVISIBLE TO EVERY CHECKER — and one was this round's own regression

**Found on the LIVE production site, 9 September 2026, in real Chrome. All three fixed.**

**1. ⚠️ THE ACCESSIBILITY FIX DEFEATED THE CSS, AND NEITHER CHANGE WAS WRONG ON ITS OWN.**
The audio player is styled `position: sticky; bottom: 0`. **It never stuck.** Measured:
`getBoundingClientRect().top` went **120 → −280 → −5382** as the page scrolled — the bar scrolled away
and never came back, on all 37 document pages, in all four viewport/theme cells.
⚠️ **The cause was established CAUSALLY, not inferred:** `bottom`-stickiness only holds a box whose flow
position is BELOW the viewport bottom. **This round moved the component ahead of `<article>` for keyboard
order** (WCAG 2.4.3 — it had been the **184th tab stop** on a bar visible from first paint), so it became
the first thing in the column and was scrolled past immediately. The reviewer built the minimal case:
identical box last in an 8000px container pins; **first, it never does.** It also ruled out
`body { overflow-x: clip }` by overriding it live.
**Fixed to `top: var(--header-h)`** — the house pattern the sidebar and table of contents already use,
which works for an element early in the flow, i.e. exactly where keyboard order wants it. ⚠️ **The two
decisions are COUPLED: if anyone moves the component back after `</article>`, `bottom` becomes correct
again and `top` stops working.** Recorded in the CSS.

**2. ⚠️ THE ZERO-OFF-ORIGIN PROPERTY WAS ALREADY GONE BEFORE THE PLAYER SHIPPED, AND THE COMMENT
JUSTIFYING THE PLAYER SAID OTHERWISE.** Every page requests `www.googletagmanager.com` and
`region1.google-analytics.com` — **GA4, deployed deliberately**, in `site/public/analytics.js` and
`BaseHead.astro`, explicitly allowed by the CloudFront CSP. ⚠️ **The reviewer attributed this carefully
rather than filing it as a regression: clean extension-free profile, zero `chrome-extension://` requests,
so it is not the WalkMe artefact a previous pass correctly attributed to machine policy.**
`AudioPlayer.astro` claimed *"the site currently makes ZERO off-origin requests. This element keeps that
property."* **False when written.** The self-hosting decision stands on its own merits — two analytics
requests is not fifteen scripts from six hosts — **but the justification was measuring against a property
the site had already given up.** Comment corrected.

**3. ⚠️ CSP SILENTLY BLOCKED A COMPONENT ON EVERY DOCUMENT PAGE — the exact trap another file in this
repo already documents.** `CiteThis.astro` used a plain Astro `<script>`; **Astro inlines a script that
small**, and production CSP is `script-src 'self'` with no `unsafe-inline`. Live: **3
`[data-cite-block]` elements, 0 copy buttons**, and a console error on every document page.
⚠️ **Its own comment said *"A bundled Astro script, not an inline one"* — correct about the policy and
wrong about what Astro does with it.** And `public/audio-player.js`'s header documents this trap in
terms: *"Inline scripts are silently blocked in production and work fine locally, because the policy is a
CloudFront response header."* **The note lived in the file that had already learned it.** Extracted to
`site/public/cite-copy.js` with `is:inline src=`, like the seven other scripts.

⚠️ **THE STANDING LESSON: none of these three is visible to any checker in this repository.** A sticky
rule that does not stick, an off-origin request, and a silently-blocked script are all *rendered*
properties. `check_links`, `check_facts`, `check_absolutes` and the build all passed throughout.
**A browser pass is not a nicety on this site; it is the only instrument for a whole class.**

### ⚠️ `scripts/speech/` IS A STALE LANDMINE — and it is the ALREADY-RECORDED `--only` trap, rediscovered

An agent reported **15 pre-rendered `scripts/speech/**/*.ssml` files embedding superseded caption text
verbatim** — including `positions__center/048.ssml` carrying *"the section says only 'a skater'"*, a
clause repaired in this round.

**Bounded, and here are the bounds, measured:** the directory holds **2,842 `.ssml` files**, is
**gitignored at `.gitignore:56`**, has **zero files tracked in git**, and its mtime is **19 August** —
three weeks stale. It is `md_to_speech.py`'s default `--out`, consumed by no script, no build step and
no workflow. **It does not ship and it does not reach a listener.**

⚠️ **BUT IT IS A LIVE TRAP FOR AGENTS, AND THIS PLAN ALREADY RECORDS IT** under *"`md_to_speech --only`
LEAVES SIBLING RENDERS STALE, and nearly produced a false finding."* **An agent that runs
`--only <doc>` and then greps `scripts/speech/` reads three-week-old text for every OTHER document** —
and every agent this round was told to render and read.

**Two remedies, and the second is the real one:**
1. **Regenerate the whole directory between waves** (a full `md_to_speech.py` run overwrites it). Cheap.
   ⚠️ **Do NOT do it mid-wave** — agents are reading it.
2. ⚠️ **Better: brief agents to render to a NAMESPACED SCRATCHPAD path, never the default.** A shared
   default output directory is shared state, and this round had eight agents writing to it. **The
   default is the defect; `--only` merely exposes it.**

### ⚠️ A SECOND COUNT DEFECT, SAME SHAPE AS THE FORECHECKING ONE, IN A DIFFERENT DOCUMENT

⚠️ **This wave found the same defect class twice, independently, in two files — which makes it a class
rather than an accident.**

The owner `content/technique/body_contact_and_battles.md` and the caption both write **three** body
prohibitions for a shot block: *"Never turn your back, never turn sideways and never lift a leg."*
**`content/positions/defender.md` carried only TWO** — it had dropped *"turn your back"* from the body
bullet, from the `Never:` facts value, and from Key Takeaway 9. ⚠️ **It would also have been stranded by
the caption cut.** Fixed in all three layers.

**The sibling instance, found the same day:** `forechecking_systems.md:863` said *"two prohibitions"*
where its near-verbatim twin at `:531` said *"three"* — the same file contradicting its own count across
two chunks.

⚠️ **THE CLASS: a passage that ENUMERATES its prohibitions, where the count and the list have drifted
apart. Nothing checks it.** A count is a claim, and it is the one part of a safety passage a listener
can verify against what follows — so when it is wrong it is wrong loudly. ⚠️ **`defender.md`'s
*"Check yourself"* Q7 asks for *"the three things you never do with your body"*, so the document was
asking a question its own answer no longer contained.**

**CENSUSED 9 September 2026, and it came back CLEAN — which SHARPENS the class rather than closing it.**
22 sites match `(two|three|four) (prohibitions|things you never)`. ⚠️ **All 22 boards sites say "two
prohibitions" for the back-to-the-wall / duck pair, and two is CORRECT for that pair.** There is no
wider count defect.

⚠️ **SO THE CLASS IS NARROWER AND MORE INTERESTING THAN "COUNTS GO WRONG". Both real instances are a
count that went STALE WHEN A SIBLING GAINED A COMPONENT:**
- `forechecking_systems.md:863` was **correct at "two"** until its twin `:531` **gained the shoulder-tip
  limb** in an earlier commit and became three. The count did not drift; **the list under the other copy
  grew.**
- `defender.md` §Blocking Shots said two where the owner says three, because the owner's third
  prohibition (*"turn your back"*) had been **dropped in compression**, not miscounted.

⚠️ **THE RULE THAT COMES OUT OF IT: a numeric enumeration is a CROSS-FILE dependency, and nothing
declares it.** Adding or removing one item from a list makes every sibling's count wrong, in a file the
editor may never open. **So: whenever you add or remove a component from an enumerated safety list,
grep the corpus for the COUNT WORD alongside the subject** — and note that a count is the one part of a
safety passage a listener can check against what follows, so when it is wrong it is wrong loudly.
⚠️ **`defender.md`'s "Check yourself" Q7 asked for "the three things you never do with your body" while
its own answer listed two.**

### ⚠️⚠️ A PHRASE-DEFINED CLASS CANNOT FIND A SITE THAT SAYS THE SAME THING IN OTHER WORDS

⚠️ **The sharpest method finding of this wave, and it invalidates the shape of the row above it.**

The `"can break your neck"` class was defined **by its phrase**, and censused at 8 sites. All four
unread ones were read and came back **SOUND** — the expected and correct outcome. **But the agent then
found a real defect at `content/technique/puck_handling.md:398`, which the census could never have
seen, because the value does not contain the phrase.**

> `Risk: Turning your back makes it a hit from behind, and even a light one could inflict a severe head
> or neck injury; ducking straightens the cervical spine, and that injury can occur at walking speed`

⚠️ ***"that injury"* has NO ANTECEDENT IN ITS OWN CLAUSE** — straightening the cervical spine is a
posture, not an injury — **so it reaches back across the semicolon to the HIT-FROM-BEHIND half.** Voiced
alone, the listener gets the walking-speed finding attached to *turning your back*, which **this
document's own Sources trailer at `:1015` says USA Hockey does not say.**

⚠️ **AND THE AGENT'S OWN FIRST PASS MISSED IT TOO** — its hand-written facts-label list omitted `Risk:`.
**It surfaced only from a full speech render.** ⚠️ **No checker can see a demonstrative with the wrong
antecedent**, and neither can a label grep that guesses the label.

**Repaired to 199/200**, with a full stop replacing the semicolon so the two mechanisms cannot bleed.
⚠️ **A cap collision was worked around, not reported, and the working-around is sound:** the block was at
**8 of 8 coaching facts** so no split was possible, and nine variants that also kept *"straightens the
cervical spine"* ran 202-229. **The anatomy survives in the body at `:14` and `:410`; nothing hedged or
sourced was trimmed.**

⚠️ **THE STANDING LESSON: a class defined by a PHRASE is a census of that phrase, not of the claim.**
The corpus-wide count of *"break your neck"* is now **9 lines, not 8 — and that is the repair, not a
regression.** **Nobody has run a corpus-wide audit for dangling antecedents or for this claim stated in
other words.** That is the open half of this row.

### ⚠️ THE BOARDS-POSTURE CENSUS, RE-DERIVED — and the answer is a RATIO, not a count

An agent's restraint at three sites rested on a figure relayed in its brief (**"16 in 108"**) which it
correctly declined to re-derive and flagged as unverified. **Re-derived by the coordinator 9 September
2026: 177 windows, 22 carrying the shoulder-tip limb.**

⚠️ **BOTH NUMBERS ARE PROPERTIES OF THEIR PATTERN, NOT OF THE CORPUS**, and neither should be quoted as
a total. Mine matched `skates parallel|forearm and hip|back to the boards/wall|never duck|chin off your
chest`. **What survives the difference is the RATIO — 12% against 15% — and that is what the restraint
actually rested on.** The limb is on a small minority of posture windows under any measure, so adding it
to every site would break the corpus norm rather than follow it. **The agent's judgement holds.**

**And the census shows the outliers are NOT where the round was looking.** `forechecking_systems.md` is
now 3 of 7 (43%) — the highest ratio in the corpus, but it is the document that discusses wall contact at
the pinch decision, and the owner `body_contact_and_battles.md` is 5 of 23. ⚠️ **The real gaps are:**

### ⚠️ OPEN — THE NHL'S OWN INDEX DISAGREES WITH ITS OWN SIGNAL TABLE, and nothing records it

Found by a commit gate re-deriving `rules_primer.md`'s new hooking material. **The NHL rulebook's signal
table at `sources/nhl_rules_layout.txt:3073` gives `29.18 | Hooking | "A tugging motion with both arms…"`.
⚠️ Its own back-of-book INDEX at `:10839` files the hooking signal at 29.17 and the icing signal at
29.18 — one lower than the table.**

⚠️ **AN EARLIER VERSION OF THIS ROW SAID THE OFFSET RUNS "THROUGHOUT". RE-MEASURED, AND THAT IS FALSE.**
`29.1`–`29.10` **agree exactly** (Boarding 29.1, Charging 29.3, Clipping 29.5, Elbowing 29.10). **The
offset begins at "Goal scored" — table 29.12 / index 29.11 — and runs to the end**: High-sticking
29.15/29.14, Holding 29.16/29.15, Holding the stick 29.17/29.16, Hooking 29.18/29.17, Icing 29.19/29.18,
Interference 29.21/29.20, Wash out 29.35/29.34. The index has **no `- signal` sub-entry under Fighting**
(table 29.11), which is where the shift begins.

⚠️ **PROOF IT IS AN OFFSET AND NOT A MISREADING:** the eight consecutive late index entries
29.25/26/27/28/30/32/33/34 map, under +1, exactly onto the table's alphabetical run Penalty shot /
Roughing / Slashing / Spearing / Time-out / Tripping / Unsportsmanlike / Wash out. **Under a zero offset
they map onto nothing coherent.**

**So the warning to record is narrower and more useful than the row first stated: a signal citation
checked against the index will look wrong for `29.12` and above, and right below it.**

**The corpus follows the TABLE, which is correct.** But nothing in `sources/README.md` records that the
NHL's index is offset, so the next agent to check a signal number against the index will find a
mismatch and may "correct" a correct citation. ⚠️ **This is a source-internal contradiction, not a corpus
defect — and it is exactly the kind of thing `sources/README.md` exists to hold.** Verify the offset is
systematic rather than a single typo, then record it there with the two line numbers.

### ⚠️⚠️ OPEN — `describe` IS A SECOND LISTENER'S LAYER, AND IT CARRIES THE CAPTION TOO

**Established from source on 9 September 2026, not inferred — two agents had reported `describe` as
"never voiced, page-only", and that is half true and misleading.**

1. **`describe` never reaches the AUDIO pipeline.** `scripts/md_to_speech.py` contains **zero** field
   accesses to `describe`; its `_image` handler reads `entry["caption"]` and nothing else (`:677-683`).
2. ⚠️ **But `describe` DOES reach a SCREEN READER.** `site/scripts/lib/rink.mjs:566-571`, `longDesc()`,
   returns `` `${describe} ${caption}` `` and `:1932-1935` emits it as `<desc>` under `role="img"`.
   Verified in the built artefact: `site/public/diagrams/dz-collapse-corner.svg` has exactly one
   `<desc>`, 2,139 characters, opening with the describe text and **ending with the caption**.
3. ⚠️⚠️ **AND THIS IS THE PART THAT CHANGES THE RANKING.** `site/src/plugins/remark-corpus.mjs:292`
   marks the `<figcaption>` **`aria-hidden`**, on the stated ground that the SVG's `<desc>` carries the
   same words. **So for a screen-reader user the `<desc>` is the ONLY route to the caption at all.**

⚠️ **A NEW SEAM NOBODY HAS SWEPT: the `describe`/`caption` JOIN.** They are announced as one continuous
utterance separated by a single space. **A negation ending a `describe` and an imperative opening a
`caption` would invert across that join — in two fields that are each individually correct.** No tool
looks at the pair, and neither of this round's caption censuses did.

⚠️ **CORRECTION TO A FIGURE THIS PLAN NEARLY CARRIED.** The `describe` population was relayed to an
agent as **269**. It is not. Measured: wide sweep **619** hits (**528** caption / **91** describe);
narrowed to em dash, semicolon or colon, **381** (**339** caption / **42** describe). ⚠️ **`describe` is
42 on the strong measure. Re-run it; do not quote this line** — it is here to kill the 269, not to
replace it with another number to copy.

**Priority: below captions** — smaller audience, and `describe` carries walk-through prose rather than
instructions — **but NOT "far below", and the join is the part to sweep first.**

### ⚠️ THE DISCRIMINATOR THAT CAME OUT OF THE CAPTION PASS — worth more than the repairs

Asked why one cardinal-rule instruction inverted and a dozen siblings did not, an agent found the rule:

> **Repair when the negation is a MAIN-CLAUSE negation immediately before the separator. Leave when it
> is embedded in a relative or subordinate clause, sits behind a MATCHED PAIR of parenthetical dashes,
> or is resolved by an intervening "so" or "but".**

⚠️ **The corpus's own convention was already doing this correctly and nobody had noticed:** every other
cardinal-rule instruction in `site/src/diagrams/` is introduced by **"so"** — *"…is a coaching choice and
not a law — …**so** find out which yours runs"* — and **that conjunction closes the negation.**
`dz-collapse-corner` was the single one with a bare imperative straight after the dash.

**Applying that rule found one more, penalty-bearing:** `goalie-rim-stop-or-clear` — *"the published
documents **do not settle** whether the suspension still stands: **assume it binds**, ask your league…"*
Inverted: *"don't assume it binds"*, telling a goaltender to assume the trapezoid restriction does not
bind. **A delay-of-game minor, and the conservative half of an unsettled question.** Repaired.

## ⚠️⚠️⚠️ TIER 0 — READABILITY AND DIAGRAMS. THE OWNER'S STANDING PRIORITY, ABOVE EVERYTHING BELOW.

**Set by the owner, 4 September 2026, and restated after a session that did not follow it.** ⚠️ **A previous
stretch spent seven gate cycles on boarding rules while this sat untouched. Rules defects that BLOCK a commit
must be cleared to ship — but they are not the priority, and chasing a blocker is not the same as choosing
the work.**

### OPEN — ⚠️ THE OWNER DOES NOT WANT LONG CAPTIONS. Set 8 September 2026, mid-round.

**Owner's words:** *"we don't want long captions or tooltips for images especially when the content
around them explains the image clearly."*

**Measured at the moment the directive arrived** (read from the build product
`site/src/data/diagrams.json`; **re-run this, never quote the line**):

| | |
|---|---|
| unique captioned units | **198** |
| total caption text | **295,428 characters** |
| median caption | **1,280 chars** |
| longest caption | **6,069 chars** — `net-front-walk-out-direction`, **4.7× the median** |
| captions over 1,500 chars | **68 — 34% of units, but 52% of all caption text** |

⚠️ **Marker placements (317) and unique captions (198) are DIFFERENT NUMBERS and the difference is the
point.** A borrowed caption is voiced **in full in every document that hosts it**, so the cost of a long
one is multiplied, not shared. `net-front-walk-out-direction` is hosted by
`technique/body_contact_and_battles.md:1055`, `positions/defender.md:217` and
`positions/goaltender.md:1126` — **6,069 characters spoken three times.** Shortening ONE caption is
therefore worth three cuts. This is the correction to the earlier D2 pricing note below, sharpened: not
merely that borrowing costs listening time, but that **the longest captions are the ones most worth
cutting because they are the ones most often borrowed.**

⚠️ **HOW TO CUT, AND IT IS NOT NEGOTIABLE.** Cut what the surrounding prose already carries. **Do NOT cut
hedges, scope flags, classification limits, citations or safety conditions to get the length down** —
that is non-negotiable 4 and it is how this project already lost a correct fact. And **"the surrounding
content explains it" must be checked in EVERY HOST**, not just the owning document: a condition that is
duplicated in `body_contact_and_battles.md` may be the ONLY statement of it a `defender.md` listener
gets. Where a caption sentence is load-bearing in one host only, **move the substance into that host's
body** rather than deleting it.

### OPEN — ⚠️ COVERAGE IS NOT SEVERABILITY. Do not cut a caption from a coverage table.

A per-host coverage table ("this material appears in all three hosts") is a **strand** test: it correctly
identifies what must NOT be cut. **It is worthless as a CUT test.** An estimate built that way was wrong
by **4×** — ≈1,220 chars predicted, **319 actual** — because a sentence can be fully duplicated elsewhere
and still be structurally load-bearing where it sits: it may carry a referent the next sentence needs, or
a book name whose removal converts a naming into a false count.

⚠️ **A count is not a neutral way to state a list.** Naming three books says nothing about the fourth;
*"three of the four"* says something false about it. An agent nearly shipped that exact conversion on a
hooking claim where the fourth book reaches the act through a different rule.

picture.** The safe cut (~1,220 chars of citation restatement duplicated in all three hosts) is being
taken now. **The remaining ~2,400 chars cannot be cut in place.**

`608(b)`, `7.5(c)`, `43.2`, `chin off your chest`, `spinal`, `walking speed`, `across the front of your
own net`, `edges are gone`. **For a goaltender reader the caption is the SOLE carrier** of the

### OPEN — make the `Never:` em-dash inversion a MECHANICAL check

⚠️ **The style guide has named this shape since round 59 as *"the single most dangerous sentence shape
this corpus has found"*, and until round 69 nobody had asked how many existed. The answer was NINE**,
three of them inverting *"head up, chin off your chest"* — the instruction that prevents a cervical
spine injury against a goal post.

**It is mechanically detectable and no existing tool sees it.** `check_facts` validates labels, lengths
and structure and all ten values pass; `check_absolutes` looks for unscoped denials; the layer test asks
whether a counterweight exists, and it does — in the same value. ⚠️ **The defect lives only in the
rendered prosody.**

**Shape of the check:** in a `Never:`, `Priority:` or `Risk:` value, flag any clause after a second em
dash that is an INSTRUCTION.

⚠️ **DO NOT DEFINE "INSTRUCTION" AS "BEGINS WITH AN IMPERATIVE VERB". That is what the round-69 census
did, and it missed a CRITICAL** — `offensive_zone_play.md:308`, whose tail begins with the noun phrase
*"skates parallel to the wall"* and which inverts *"head up and chin off your chest"*. It is the style
guide's own printed worked example of the defect, and the census walked past it.

⚠️ **A count produced by a heuristic is a property of the heuristic, not of the corpus.** The round-69
census reported "nine" when it meant "nine that a verb-led regex could see". The style guide's own
find-rate history — **predicted 9 / found 33**, **predicted 11 / found 26**, and an agent that missed one
on the verb *"aim"* — says every such scan undercounts. **Flag negation-then-dash and READ every tail.**

⚠️ **A WORKLIST, NOT A GATE, and the reason is measured: of 579 such values carrying an em dash, the
overwhelming majority introduce a REASON and are correct.** A crude imperative-verb regex also produced
at least one false positive (*"play does not stop until…"*, where *"play"* is a noun). **Read every hit.
A sweep here would strip correct reasons out of hundreds of values.**

### OPEN — build an ORDERING check over the ` ```facts ` blocks

⚠️ **The layer test asks whether a counterweight EXISTS. Nothing asks whether it arrives IN TIME.**

Proposed: *is any `Never:` or counterweight line more than two units downstream of the hazard it
corrects, with a permission in between?* Run over all 830 blocks.

**Measured instance** (`offensive_zone_play.md:799-803`): a listener hears *"pinch when the winger is
facing the glass"*, then two unrelated units, then *"take the player"*, and only then the rule — while
the body's actual disambiguation (*"it tells you they cannot escape with the puck, not that you may hit
them"*) reaches **no facts line at all**. ⚠️ **Every existing check passes this block**, because it
contains both the hazard and an answer, in any order.

**A worklist, not a gate** — legitimate blocks will order a hazard before its answer.

`defending_the_rush.md` §Target distances shipped **5,488 characters of provenance against 1,714 of

**The test that decides whether a disclosure belongs in the body — and it is a test, not a judgement:**

1. ⚠️ **Is it duplicated in the Sources trailer?** If yes, relocating it loses nothing and non-negotiable
   4 is not engaged. **This is the step that was always missing from "never strip a disclosure".**
2. ⚠️ **Does the evidence survive the renderer?** Figure numbers become *"eight point one to eight point
   three"*. A listener cannot hold or check them. **Evidence that cannot be heard is not disclosure, it

3. **Does the renderer flag it `Important.`?** If a publisher's contents list is being announced as
   important mid-lesson, it is in the wrong layer.

**Keep the name and the hedge in the body; move the working to the trailer.** *"A reader wants to know
who wrote it, not how we worked out who wrote it."*

⚠️ **Run this ratio over every document. The owner's caption directive and this are the same disease.**

wrong landmark.** Both are plausible and this is not resolvable by geometry alone — it needs
`content-reviewer` or `rules-verifier` on that section. ⚠️ **Do not "fix" it by moving a coordinate**:
the diagram asserts no coordinate for this branch, deliberately, so nothing is currently shipping
wrong in the picture. **The defect, if it is one, is in the prose.**

### ⚠️ CORRECTION TO MY OWN D2 PRICING — BORROWING IS FREE TO WRITE AND NOT FREE TO HEAR

Two `positions/` agents, working independently and without contact, **both chose to borrow existing
diagrams rather than author new ones** — five borrows into `defender.md`, six into `center.md`, and
**zero new diagrams between them.** Their reasoning was the same and it is sound: the corpus's own
preference is *"borrowing beats duplicating"*, the captions are already reviewed under their owning
documents, and authoring a new rule-bearing caption for a safety-critical section inside an 800-char
budget risks shipping a hedge bare.

⚠️ **But my ceiling analysis priced new diagrams at the cost of writing them, and that was wrong.
A borrowed caption is voiced in full in every document that hosts it.** Borrowing avoids the
authoring cost, the geometry risk and the review cost. **It avoids none of the listening cost — and
because legacy captions run to the old median, a borrow costs MORE per marker than a newly written
one.**

Measured on `defender.md`: five borrows totalling **9,080 characters — 1,707 words, about 11.4
minutes of extra speech on one page.** Two of them (`net-front-walk-out-direction` 2,678,
`goalie-rim-stop-or-clear` 2,670) are **more than double** the corpus median. The page moved from
**10.9% to 15.3% caption.**

**Corpus-wide, after today's diagram work:** 286 → **304 markers**, 80,382 → **84,616 caption
words**, **7.5% → 8.0%** of spoken text, 8.9 → **9.4 hours**. ⚠️ **These figures were WRONG in an
earlier draft (305 / 8.1% / 19) because the count used a bare `diagram:` grep that matched a prose
sentence — `game_management.md:302`. Count markers with an ANCHORED `^!\[\](diagram:…)$` or not at
all.** Still inside the 10% ceiling, but **18 markers consumed a sixth of the
headroom** — where 18 newly written captions at today's 601–838
would have consumed about half that.

**So the rule for the rest of D2 is:** borrowing is still right for correctness and consistency, and
it is **not** the cheap option for a listener. **Where a borrowed caption is far above the median,
weigh the borrow against writing a short one** — and count borrows against the ceiling exactly like
new diagrams, which the original entry did not say.

### ⚠️ EVIDENCE THAT THE GAP CENSUS OVER-COUNTS: goaltender.md scored 41 gaps and yielded ZERO

An agent was sent to draw the spatial gaps in `positions/goaltender.md` — **41 undiagrammed sections
by census, the largest count in `positions/`**. It read all 1,434 lines and **drew nothing**, with a
section-by-section justification. That is the correct answer and it is recorded here as evidence,
not as a failure.

**Why nothing qualified:** *the ready stance*, *squaring up*, *on your feet*, *on your knees* and
**post integration (VH and RVH)** are all **body mechanics** — pad and torso orientation relative to
the goaltender's own body. ⚠️ **This corpus draws a goaltender as a bare `G` glyph with no shape
around it. A glyph cannot show a pad seal.** *Tracking the puck* is eye mechanics; *the butterfly is
a tool, not a religion* is doctrine; *the load on your hips* is owned by
`conditioning_and_recovery.md`; *6-on-5* and *penalty kill* are rules-dominated and their spatial
content is already drawn by `goalie-playing-the-angle`, `goalie-front-door-back-door` and
`special_teams.mjs`'s `pk-*` set.

**The document already carries 10 goaltender-specific diagrams plus 10 borrowed**, covering depth,
angle, the arc, safe outlets, the trapezoid rim, breakaway retreat, tip lanes, rebound direction,
the fifty-fifty race and odd-man rushes — **every spatial axis the position has.**

⚠️ **So "41 gaps" in the census meant "41 sections without a marker", NOT "41 diagrams owed."** The
census counts headings; only reading decides. **Treat the 917 figure accordingly** — this is the
first document where the filter has actually been applied, and it removed 100% of them.

**The agent's own honest caveat, worth keeping:** a reviewer applying a looser bar could justify one
diagram for *"Playing bigger and deeper through traffic"* or *"6-on-5 with your net empty"*. It
judged caption-budget discipline and duplication-avoidance to outweigh that. **That is a judgment
call, not a certainty**, and it is the right one to revisit only if the ceiling turns out to have
room.

### ⚠️⚠️ D2 HAS A CEILING, AND IT IS ~100 NEW DIAGRAMS — NOT 917

**Priced 6 September 2026** from the measured caption load (286 markers, 80,382 spoken caption
words, 90.0 hours, **7.5% of everything the corpus speaks**), at the observed 281 caption words per
marker:

| new diagrams | added speech | caption total | **captions as share of spoken text** |
|---|---|---|---|
| +100 | +3.1 h | 12.1 h | **9.9%** |
| +300 | +9.4 h | 18.3 h | **14.3%** |
| **+917** (every gap) | **+28.6 h** | **37.6 h** | ⚠️ **25.5%** |

⚠️ **Filling every gap would make a quarter of everything a listener hears be diagram caption.**
That is the exact pathology already flagged as a defect in `off-the-ice/how_to_watch_hockey.md`,
which sits at **27.7%** and is the worst document in the corpus. **"Draw a diagram for every
section" is self-defeating: it reproduces corpus-wide the very condition we have recorded as a
readability failure in one document.**

**So D2 is DONE when the high-value gaps are drawn, not when the gap list is empty.** The working
ceiling is **about 100 new diagrams**, which holds captions under 10% of spoken text. Priority
order, from the owner's own words (*"especially all sections in the positions part of the sight"*):

1. **`positions/`** — 93 gaps, the owner's named priority, and the four sections they named by hand.
2. The `systems/` gaps where the section is a named, spatial structure.
3. `D3`'s ~31 Overview diagrams — **counted against the same ceiling**, since they are markers too.

⚠️ **And the ceiling is a reason to keep captions SHORT, not a reason to draw badly.** Every new
caption written this round has come in **under 900 characters against a median of 1,303** (the
zone-entry five at 735–838, the `D3` pilot at 624). **If new diagrams are captioned at half the
legacy median, ~100 of them cost about 1.6 hours rather than 3.1.** The budget is the lever, and it
is already working.

**What this does NOT license:** deleting a legacy caption to make room. The long ones are long
because they carry qualifications and safety counterweights — see the R5 entry.

### OPEN — `check_pointers` run 3 September 2026: 3 hits in 37 documents, ONE of them real

**Ran after round 60's content edits. The layer is in good shape — but read all three, do not sweep.**

1. ⚠️ **REAL, and the only one worth fixing.** `rules_primer.md` — *"…near-identical wording, but not
   identical: **see the note below**."* **A listener cannot see a note below.** The note is voiced content,
   so the substance survives; what dangles is the deictic. **Fix by naming what the note SAYS rather than
   where it sits.** ⚠️ **NOT DONE — the file was under live `safety-reviewer` review when this was found,
   and editing it would have made that report stale. Do it in the next wave.**
2. **LEGITIMATE, leave alone.** `playing_without_the_puck.md` — *"Both computations are set out in full in
   **the written** Notes on verification section."* ⚠️ **The word "written" is doing exactly the job this
   class needs**: it tells the listener the detail is in the written version rather than pretending they
   can reach it. **This is the well-formed shape of a site-aimed pointer, and it should be the model for
   fixing hit 1.**
3. **Reported as ambiguous by the tool itself.** `rules_primer.md` — the sentence about amendments *"not in
   this table at all"*, in a **MIXED document** (1 table voiced, 3 dropped) where the tool cannot tell
   which table the sentence means. ⚠️ **Read the rendered SSML before touching it** — and note the sentence
   says what is NOT in the table, which may be sound regardless of whether the table is voiced.

### OPEN — a caption can be CORRECT AND UNLISTENABLE, and nothing checks for it

⚠️ **Measured this round on a repaired caption that every rule check passed.** Its final spoken unit ran
**138 words**; the rules clause alone ran **84 words**, carrying **five rule numbers across three books**
and **two different escalation logics**, voiced alone with a 300 ms break either side to someone with no
picture and no text.

**The verifier's judgement, which is the finding:** *"The old caption's failure was that a listener heard
the wrong price. This one's is that a listener hears no price at all. **That is a different failure, not
a smaller one.**"* What a listener retains is the last thing said — here, a list of five fouls with no
verdict attached, arriving after the number that mattered had gone.

⚠️ **No tool in `scripts/` measures this, and the verifier said plainly that it reached the finding by
counting words and reading the caption aloud in its head** — *"not a check anyone can automate and not
one any of the eleven scripts performs."*

**The remedy that worked, and it generalises:** ⚠️ **rule numbers belong in the ` ```facts ` block and the
body, where a reader can stop and re-read. A caption is heard ONCE.** Carry the tiers in **words**, one
book per spoken unit, **floor first**; where a route is genuinely three steps long, point at the section
— `check_pointers.py` treats a pointer at the site as legitimate.

**Whether to build a spoken-length worklist for the caption layer is open.** ⚠️ **If one is built it must
be a WORKLIST, not a gate, and must never gain a `--strict`** — a long caption is often correct, because
a picture with six players genuinely needs six sentences to describe, and no tool can tell a dense
caption from an overloaded one.

### OPEN — a caption whose BODY says "this document" cannot safely be borrowed

⚠️ **The renderer announces a borrowed caption's owner — `"Diagram, from forechecking systems. …"` — but
that only fixes ATTRIBUTION. It does not fix a caption whose own text says *"this document"*.**

Found while an agent was choosing reuse candidates. It **rejected `entry-delay-curl`** for a section that
otherwise wanted it, because its caption reads *"this document has no figure for what share of wasted
entries that accounts for"* — and *"this document"* means **`zone_entries.md`**, not the document a
listener is currently in. **Borrowed into another file, the caption makes a claim about the wrong
document's evidence base.**

**The agent screened its two accepted reuses for the same wording and reported doing so.** ⚠️ **That
screen is not written down anywhere, no tool performs it, and the reuse pattern is the corpus's cheapest
readability win** — 9 borrows exist and the `technique/` and `off-the-ice/` gaps will be closed largely
by borrowing.

**Two candidate remedies, both cheap, neither chosen:**
1. **A worklist** over every caption and `describe` for document-relative phrasing — *"this document"*,
   *"this guide"*, *"the section"*, *"above"*, *"below"*, *"the next diagram"*. ⚠️ **Note the last three
   are a DIFFERENT hazard already measured this round: two captions carry ordering dependencies
   (*"against the same puck carrier as the 2-1-2 above"*, *"the next diagram shows theirs"*) that resolve
   **only** because the embedding document happens to place the pair adjacently and in that order.
   **Nothing mechanical checks it, and it is invisible in the source.**
2. **A convention:** a caption states its own evidence limits in terms of the claim, never in terms of
   *"this document"* — the same rule the corpus already applies to prose under non-negotiable 6.

⚠️ **Do not sweep either pattern.** A caption saying *"the section covers the reception separately"* is
legitimate where it is not borrowed, and an ordering reference is legitimate in the document that owns
both diagrams.

### ⚠️ STANDING GUIDANCE — AGENTS MUST NAMESPACE SCRATCHPAD FILES

**Measured twice in one round, by two agents that each lost work.** The session scratchpad is **shared
between concurrent agents**, and the obvious filenames collide.

> *"I wrote `scratchpad/render.mjs`; a later run of it rendered another agent's diagrams at widths of
> 11500/8927/9514 — **another agent's script under my filename. Mine may equally have destroyed
> theirs.**"*

A second agent independently reported: *"my first scratch render script was **silently overwritten by
another agent** at the shared session scratchpad path and rendered a different agent's diagrams under my
command."*

⚠️ **Neither agent was told it had been clobbered. Both noticed only because the OUTPUT was wrong** — one
saw impossible widths, the other saw diagrams it had not written. **A clobbered script that happens to
produce plausible output would not have been caught at all**, and a diagram agent's whole verification
rests on looking at what it rendered.

**The instruction, for every brief from here:** ⚠️ **write scratch files to a private subdirectory named
for your task (`scratchpad/<task>/`), never to the scratchpad root.** CLAUDE.md already says *"scratchpad,
not `/tmp`"* for secrecy reasons; **this adds that the scratchpad root is itself contended.**

### OPEN — two RENDERER defects seen in Chrome-rendered pixels, both with the cause located

⚠️ **Both are in `site/scripts/lib/rink.mjs` — SHARED library code — so they must change BETWEEN waves,
and a fix needs a rebuild plus re-verification of every diagram it touches.**

**1. The puck is drawn inside a player glyph, over the identifying letter.** Seen in
`winger-offensive-zone-patches`: glyph `r=2.9`, puck `r=1.1`, centres **2.24 ft** apart — **80% of the puck
disc inside the glyph**. ⚠️ **Two notations degrade at once: an OPEN circle (our team) reads as partly
filled (opposition), and the letter is eaten.**
⚠️ **Cause, `rink.mjs:1739-1741`: the puck is drawn LAST, unconditionally, with NO avoidance — while the
label placer THREE LINES ABOVE builds an explicit `avoid` list of `{w:7,h:8}` boxes from those same
players.** **The remedy already exists in the file; the puck was simply never given it.**
⚠️ **Corpus-wide: an agent measured ~20 diagrams with puck-on-glyph overlap, up to −2.25 ft.** **Five were
fixed in one module this round by moving pucks; the convention question was never settled.** **Fixing the
renderer settles it once instead of twenty times.**

**2. Zone labels overflow their zone and ERASE rink markings.** ⚠️ **`rink.mjs:1311-1318` places the label
at the polygon centroid with a FIXED `stroke-width="1.1"` white halo while `font-size` scales per
diagram.** **Corpus-wide: 509 haloed labels, halo-to-type ratio 18.9% → 37.5%.**
**Four instances seen in Chrome-rendered pixels:** *"the high slot"* rendered **23.3 ft wide inside a 15 ft
zone**, erasing that zone's own dashed borders · a halo **severing the blue line** in a clean notch in
`angling-your-route` — ⚠️ **NOT pre-existing: this diagram is NEW IN THE ROUND-60 COMMIT
(`body_contact_and_battles.mjs:190`, embedded at `body_contact_and_battles.md:200`, absent from
`HEAD:diagrams.json`), so that commit SHIPS a picture erasing a segment of the blue line.** ⚠️ **`commit-gate`
asked for this distinction explicitly, because filing a self-introduced instance under generic renderer
behaviour makes the next round rank it LOWER than it deserves.** **It was judged a rendering blemish rather
than a false claim, which is why it did not block — but the other three instances are pre-existing and this
one is not, and that is the difference between inheriting a defect and adding one** · a halo painting out a segment of the **goal
crease** · a doubled ghost on `strong-side-and-weak-side`.
⚠️ **Erasing the boundary of the very region a label names is information loss about that region's
extent.** **The fix is half-written already: the renderer computes the label's width at `:1315` for
`zoneReserve` and then DISCARDS it** — compare it against the polygon extent, and scale the halo with
`font-size`.

**3. Smaller, same file:** the `danger: true` flag switches fill and stroke at `:1325-1326` but
`:1317` hard-codes the label `fill="${P.home}"`, ⚠️ **so the corpus's first red zone carries a blue
label** — the one notation collision that flag was added to prevent, reintroduced at the label. **The
region still reads unmistakably red, so no reader is misled.**

**4. Not renderer, but same review:** `analytics.js` and `audio-player.js` **ship and are loaded by zero
pages** — `analytics.js` is a GA4 bootstrap that no-ops without a meta tag **absent from every page** —
⚠️ **yet both are in the service worker's PRECACHE array, so every install downloads two dead files.**
**And the table scroll wrappers' ARIA label and `tabindex="0"` are unconditional, though the VISUAL
affordance is correct** (`background-attachment` shows the fade only when scrollable).
